Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- In a time of economic turmoil, most Americans are being frugal with their money, but one freshman congressman is taking cost-cutting to a new level. Rep. Jason Chaffetz unfolds the cot that fits into a closet in his office. Newly elected Rep. Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, opted out of renting an apartment in Washington, instead deciding on a cot in his office every night. "I will save $1,500 a month doing this," Chaffetz said. "I get paid a very handsome salary, no doubt about it, but you know, I've got expenses and a future for my kids and my family, too. " In a stroke of luck, Chaffetz was one of the few freshmen members of Congress to have the chance at an office with a window when he drew number six out of 55 in the office lottery. His office in the Longworth House Building comes with a half-bathroom, a closet that fits a cot, and what he calls his "breakfast nook" where he stores Fig Newtons, granola bars and mixed nuts.  Watch more on the thrifty congressman » . The building also has a gym with a shower room, where Chaffetz starts his day about 5:45 each morning. "My home is in Utah. My wife and kids are there," he said. "I'm here to work." Cutting out travel to and from the office allows Chaffetz more time to serve his constituents and return more of their e-mail and phone calls, he said. The savings are certainly a plus for the congressman, who has three children to provide for, car payments and a mortgage to pay. But Chaffetz said his decision had a larger meaning. "We are now $10 trillion in debt. $10 trillion. Those are expenses that have to be paid at some point," he said. If he can tighten his belt in these tough economic times, Chaffetz said, Congress should be able to as well. "Our country has to learn to do more with less," he added. Although he is a relatively unknown freshman in the House, word of Chaffetz's sleeping arrangement is spreading. Republican Rep. Judy Biggert of Illinois, whose office is adjacent to Chaffetz's, said he isn't the first to sleep in his office, and he won't be the last. "This is a job that you have to have, really, two homes. One in your district where you're there on the weekends and then one here during the week, and it's expensive," Rep. Biggert said. "I'm really glad we have a neighbor here to make sure that the neighborhood is safe at night when we're not here," she joked, adding that Chaffetz is actually projecting the right image of the Republican Party by being a "fiscal conservative." Chaffetz said he is finally getting used to sleeping on his not-so-comfortable cot, but that doesn't mean he rests easy at night. "My biggest challenge is what goes on in the hallway at night," Chaffetz said. "There's this cleaning machine that comes down the hall at night. And it's got that obnoxious beep, beep, beep." Despite the din, Chaffetz has no plans to search for another form of housing -- unless his back gives out. "I've got to keep my back in check, but so far, so good," Chaffetz joked. "But look, our troops are sleeping on a lot worse than this."

Newly elected Rep. Jason Chaffetz, R-Utah, has opted not to rent an apartment in Washington. Instead, he sleeps each night on a cot that folds into a closet in his office.

“I will save $1,500 a month doing this,” Chaffetz said. “I get paid a very handsome salary, no doubt about it, but, you know, I’ve got expenses and a future for my kids and my family, too.”

In a stroke of luck, Chaffetz was among the few freshman members of Congress to have a chance at an office with a window after drawing number six out of 55 in the office lottery.

His office in the Longworth House Office Building includes a half-bathroom, a closet large enough to hold a cot, and what he calls his “breakfast nook,” where he stores Fig Newtons, granola bars, and mixed nuts.

Watch more on the thrifty congressman »

The building also has a gym with a shower room, where Chaffetz begins his day at about 5:45 each morning.

“My home is in Utah. My wife and kids are there,” he said. “I’m here to work.”

Eliminating the commute to and from the office gives Chaffetz more time to serve his constituents and respond to more of their emails and phone calls, he said.

The savings are certainly a benefit for the congressman, who has three children to support, car payments, and a mortgage. But Chaffetz said his decision carries a broader meaning.

“We are now $10 trillion in debt. $10 trillion. Those are expenses that have to be paid at some point,” he said.

If he can tighten his belt during these difficult economic times, Chaffetz said, Congress should be able to do the same.

“Our country has to learn to do more with less,” he added.

Although he is a relatively unknown freshman in the House, word of Chaffetz’s sleeping arrangement is spreading.

Republican Rep. Judy Biggert of Illinois, whose office is adjacent to Chaffetz’s, said he is not the first member to sleep in his office—and he will not be the last.

“This is a job that you have to have, really, two homes. One in your district, where you’re there on the weekends, and then one here during the week, and it’s expensive,” Biggert said.

“I’m really glad we have a neighbor here to make sure that the neighborhood is safe at night when we’re not here,” she joked, adding that Chaffetz is projecting the right image of the Republican Party by being a “fiscal conservative.”

Chaffetz said he is finally becoming accustomed to sleeping on his less-than-comfortable cot, but that does not mean he rests easily at night.

“My biggest challenge is what goes on in the hallway at night,” Chaffetz said. “There’s this cleaning machine that comes down the hall at night. And it’s got that obnoxious beep, beep, beep.”

Despite the noise, Chaffetz has no plans to seek other housing—unless his back gives out.

“I’ve got to keep my back in check, but so far, so good,” Chaffetz joked. “But look, our troops are sleeping on a lot worse than this.”

WASHINGTON (CNN) — As financial uncertainty prompts many Americans to watch their spending, first-term Rep. Jason Chaffetz is embracing an unusually strict approach to saving money.

The Utah Republican has chosen not to lease a Washington apartment. Instead, he sleeps each night on a folding cot that can be stored inside his congressional office closet.

Chaffetz estimates the arrangement reduces his monthly expenses by $1,500. Although he acknowledges that members of Congress receive generous pay, he says he still has financial responsibilities and wants to plan for his wife and three children.

Chaffetz was fortunate when new House members selected their offices by lottery. He drew sixth among 55 freshmen, giving him one of the limited opportunities to choose a room with a window. Located in the Longworth House Office Building, the space includes a half-bath, a closet large enough for the cot and an area he jokingly refers to as his “breakfast nook.” There, he keeps snacks such as Fig Newtons, mixed nuts and granola bars.

The building also contains a gym and showers. Chaffetz begins his mornings there at approximately 5:45.

He says Utah remains his true home because that is where his wife and children live. His purpose in Washington, he explains, is to work. By eliminating a daily commute, he believes he has more time to help constituents and answer additional telephone calls and e-mails.

The reduced housing cost is also helpful because Chaffetz must support three children while paying a mortgage and making car payments. However, he says the choice is intended to convey a broader message.

Pointing to the nation’s $10 trillion debt, Chaffetz argues that the money will eventually have to be repaid. In his view, if he can reduce his own spending during difficult economic conditions, Congress should be capable of doing the same. He says the United States must become better at accomplishing more with fewer resources.

Though Chaffetz is still a little-known newcomer to the House, information about his office sleeping arrangement has begun to circulate. Illinois Republican Rep. Judy Biggert, who works in the neighboring office, noted that other lawmakers have slept at work before him and that others will likely do so in the future.

Biggert explained that serving in Congress effectively requires maintaining two residences: one in a lawmaker’s home district for weekends and another in Washington during the workweek. That setup, she said, is costly.

She joked that having Chaffetz nearby overnight makes the area safer after everyone else leaves. More seriously, she added that his behavior presents an appropriate image for Republicans by demonstrating fiscal conservatism.

Chaffetz says he is gradually adjusting to the cot despite its lack of comfort, although nighttime sleep is not always peaceful. His main problem is activity in the corridor, particularly a cleaning machine that travels through the hallway while repeatedly making a loud beeping sound.

Even with the noise, he does not intend to find different accommodations unless the cot begins causing serious trouble for his back. So far, he says, his back is holding up. He also points out that American military personnel often sleep in conditions far worse than his.

The Utah Republican says the unusual arrangement is an effort to save money during the economic downturn and avoid maintaining a second home more than 2,000 miles from his family.

Chaffetz, elected in 2008 to represent Utah’s 3rd Congressional District, sleeps in his House office and uses the congressional gym to shower before beginning his workday. His wife and children remain in Utah, and he returns home when the congressional schedule allows.

Washington is consistently ranked among the nation’s most expensive housing markets, with even modest apartments near the Capitol costing well over $1,000 a month. Chaffetz has said paying rent for a place he would use only a few nights a week did not make financial sense.

The arrangement also fits the fiscal-conservative image Chaffetz brought to Congress. He campaigned on reducing government spending and has argued that lawmakers should demonstrate the same restraint they ask of taxpayers.

Still, the sight of a member of Congress sleeping at work may draw mixed reactions. Rank-and-file lawmakers earn $174,000 a year, far above the income of the average American household. But members are also responsible for maintaining residences in their home districts while living part time in the Washington area.

Chaffetz is not the first lawmaker to turn a congressional office into makeshift living quarters. Other members, particularly those who live far from Washington or travel home frequently, have adopted similar routines.

For the freshman congressman, the sparse accommodations are less about comfort than convenience. At the end of a late night on Capitol Hill, home is only a few steps from his desk.
